title: Fundamental Rights and Fundamental Duties
summary: Rights are claims of an individual that are essential for his or her development and are recognised by society or the State. A duty is something one is expected or required to do. Rights and duties are 'two wheels of the chariot of life': my right brings an obligation to respect the same right of others — if I have the right to use a public park, it is my duty not to deny it to others.

The most important rights are written in the Constitution and are justiciable — enforceable through courts; a law that violates them can be declared invalid. Originally there were seven; the Right to Property was removed in 1978 by the 44th Amendment and is now only a legal right. Today there are six.

1. Right to Equality (Articles 14–18): equality before law; no discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth (special provisions allowed for women and children); equality of opportunity in public employment (with reservation for SC, ST and OBC); abolition of untouchability — practising it in any form is a punishable offence; abolition of titles like 'Sir' and 'Rai Bahadur' (national awards such as Bharat Ratna, Padma awards and gallantry awards are not titles).

2. Right to Freedom (Articles 19–22): Article 19 gives six freedoms — speech and expression; to assemble peacefully without arms; to form associations and unions; to move freely throughout India; to reside and settle anywhere in India; to practise any profession, trade or business. The State may impose reasonable restrictions in the interest of the sovereignty, integrity and security of India, public order, decency, morality, friendly relations with foreign states, or to prevent contempt of court, defamation and incitement; only courts decide what is reasonable. Article 20: protection in respect of conviction (no punishment for an act that was not an offence then, no double punishment, no forced self-incrimination). Article 21: no one can be deprived of life or personal liberty except by procedure established by law. Article 22: an arrested person must be told the grounds, may consult a lawyer and must be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours (except under preventive detention).

3. Right against Exploitation (Articles 23–24): traffic in human beings (buying and selling people), begar (forced labour without payment) and other forced labour are prohibited and punishable; no child below 14 may be employed in factories, mines or hazardous work.

4. Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25–28): India is a secular state with no religion of its own. Everyone has freedom of conscience and to profess, practise and propagate religion — but not to convert by force or allurement, and inhuman practices like sati are banned; restrictions for public order, morality and health. Religious groups may set up institutions, manage their own affairs and own property. No one can be forced to pay taxes for promoting a particular religion. No religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained by the State, and no one can be compelled to attend it elsewhere.

5. Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29–30): any minority with a distinct language, script or culture may conserve it; no one can be denied admission to a State-aided institution on grounds of religion, race, caste or language; minorities (religious or linguistic, at national or state level) may establish and run educational institutions and must not be discriminated against in grants.

6. Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32): if any fundamental right is violated, a citizen can directly approach the Supreme Court, which can issue directions, orders and writs. Dr. Ambedkar called it the heart and soul of the Constitution, because it makes all other rights real.

Right to Education: Article 21A was added in 2002 by the 86th Amendment, making free and compulsory education for children of 6–14 years a fundamental right; it became enforceable with the Right to Education Act, 2009.

The UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948 (equality before law, life, liberty, free movement, education, freedom of religion, assembly and so on). Many of these are Fundamental Rights in our Constitution; others are in the Directive Principles. The National Human Rights Commission was set up in 1993 to protect human rights in India. Human rights are universal, fundamental and absolute.

The original Constitution had no duties. Ten Fundamental Duties were added in 1976 by the 42nd Amendment: (1) abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals, institutions, the National Flag and National Anthem; (2) cherish the noble ideals of the freedom struggle; (3) uphold the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India; (4) defend the country and render national service; (5) promote harmony and brotherhood and renounce practices derogatory to women; (6) value our composite culture; (7) protect the natural environment — forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife; (8) develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry; (9) safeguard public property and abjure violence; (10) strive for excellence. An eleventh duty was added after the RTE Act: parents and guardians must provide education to children of 6–14 years. Duties are non-justiciable — not enforceable by courts — and act as a code of conduct; some are vague.

vsa: Under which Article was the Right to Education included in the Fundamental Rights, and why?

It was included as Article 21A in 2002 by the 86th Amendment, so that all children of 6–14 years (and their parents) could claim free and compulsory education as a fundamental right, a major step towards making India free of illiteracy.
April 2026

or: In which year was the Right to Education Act passed, and what does it aim to achieve for children in India?
It was passed in 2009. It aims to ensure that every child between 6 and 14 years who is out of school goes to school and receives free, compulsory, quality education as a right.

vsa: Why has untouchability been made a punishable offence under law in India? Explain.

Untouchability denied millions of people equal status and dignity because of their caste or occupation. To uplift them socially and establish equality, the Constitution abolished it (Article 17) and made its practice in any form a punishable offence.
April 2026
When was the National Human Rights Commission established, and why was it set up?

It was established in 1993 by the Government of India to guarantee that Indian citizens enjoy human rights — to inquire into violations and protect the rights to life, liberty, equality and dignity recognised in the Constitution and international declarations.
April 2026
Mention any two restrictions imposed on the Right to Freedom.

(1) Freedom of speech and expression may be restricted in the interest of the sovereignty, integrity and security of India, public order, decency or morality, or to prevent defamation and contempt of court. (2) The freedom to assemble must be peaceful and without arms and can be restricted for public order.
October 2025

or: Explain any two provisions of the Right against Exploitation.
(1) Traffic in human beings, begar and other forced labour are prohibited and punishable. (2) No child below 14 years can be employed in any factory, mine or hazardous work.

vsa: Describe the importance of human rights in the Indian Constitution.

Many human rights in the UN Universal Declaration (1948) — equality, life and liberty, freedom of religion, assembly and movement — are included as justiciable Fundamental Rights, so the government must protect them; others are in the Directive Principles. The NHRC (1993) safeguards them.
April 2024

or: (1) To abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem. (2) To protect and improve the natural environment, including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife.

vsa: Explain the relationship between rights and duties.

Rights and duties are complementary: every right brings a duty to respect the same right of others. If I have the right to life, others have a duty not to harm me; if I have the right to use public places, I have the duty not to deny them to others.
April 2022
Describe any two freedoms given in the Indian Constitution.

(1) Freedom of speech and expression — to express views freely, subject to reasonable restrictions. (2) Freedom to move freely and reside in any part of India. (Others: to assemble peacefully, form associations, and practise any profession.)
October 2024
sa: How many freedoms have been provided by Article 19 of the Indian Constitution? Explain any three.

Six freedoms. (1) Freedom of speech and expression — to express opinions through speech, writing or media, subject to restrictions for security, public order and morality. (2) Freedom to assemble peacefully and without arms — to hold meetings and processions. (3) Freedom to practise any profession or carry on any occupation, trade or business — subject to qualifications the State may lay down. (Also: to form associations, move freely, and reside anywhere in India.)

or: How many Fundamental Rights are given to Indian citizens? Explain any three.

Six. (1) Right to Equality — equality before law, no discrimination, abolition of untouchability and titles. (2) Right against Exploitation — ban on human trafficking, begar and child labour below 14. (3) Right to Constitutional Remedies — the right to approach the Supreme Court (Article 32) if any right is violated. (Also: Right to Freedom, Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights.)

sa: Describe the 'Right to Equality' as one of the important Fundamental Rights.

(1) Equality before law and equal protection of laws — no one is above the law. (2) No discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth; equal access to shops, wells, roads; equal opportunity in public employment, with reservation for SC, ST and OBC. (3) Untouchability is abolished and punishable, and titles like 'Sir' and 'Rai Bahadur' are abolished.
Explain the provisions under the 'Right against Exploitation'.

(1) Traffic in human beings — buying and selling people, especially women and children — is prohibited. (2) Begar and other forms of forced labour are banned and punishable. (3) Children below 14 cannot be employed in factories, mines or hazardous work, so that they can enjoy childhood and get education.
How does the Right to Freedom of Religion give every religious group freedom to manage its religious affairs? Explain.

Subject to public order, morality and health, every religious group may (1) establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes, (2) manage its own affairs in matters of religion, and (3) own, acquire and administer movable and immovable property according to law. The State cannot favour any religion, as India is secular.
'The Right to Constitutional Remedies is the most important fundamental right.' Justify.

(1) It makes all other rights enforceable — without it they would be mere declarations. (2) Any citizen whose right is violated can directly approach the Supreme Court (Article 32) or a High Court, which can issue writs and orders. (3) It stops the legislature and executive from curbing rights; Dr. Ambedkar called it the heart and soul of the Constitution.
Explain the cultural and educational rights of minorities.

(1) Any minority with a distinct language, script or culture has the right to conserve it. (2) No citizen can be denied admission to a State-run or aided institution on grounds of religion, race, caste or language. (3) Religious and linguistic minorities may establish and administer educational institutions, and the State cannot discriminate against them in giving aid.
la: Explain the Right to Freedom of Religion mentioned in the Indian Constitution in six points.

(1) India is a secular state with no official religion. (2) Every person has freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate any religion. (3) Conversion by force or allurement and inhuman practices like human/animal sacrifice and sati are not allowed; the State may restrict this right for public order, morality and health and regulate secular activities linked to religion. (4) Every religious group may set up institutions, manage its religious affairs and own property. (5) No one can be forced to pay taxes used for promoting a particular religion. (6) No religious instruction is given in institutions wholly maintained by the State, and no one can be compelled to attend religious instruction or worship elsewhere (a minor needs a guardian's consent). Foreigners also enjoy this right.

or: Explain any six Fundamental Duties mentioned in the Indian Constitution.

(1) To abide by the Constitution and respect the National Flag and National Anthem. (2) To cherish the noble ideals of the freedom struggle. (3) To uphold the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India and defend the country when called upon. (4) To promote harmony and brotherhood and renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women. (5) To protect the natural environment and value our composite culture. (6) To develop scientific temper, safeguard public property, abjure violence and strive for excellence; parents must educate children of 6–14 years. They were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) and are non-justiciable.

la: Explain the six Fundamental Rights guaranteed by the Indian Constitution.

(1) Right to Equality (Art. 14–18): equality before law, no discrimination, equal opportunity in jobs, abolition of untouchability and titles. (2) Right to Freedom (Art. 19–22): six freedoms, protection in conviction, life and personal liberty, safeguards on arrest; Article 21A gives free education to 6–14-year-olds. (3) Right against Exploitation (Art. 23–24): no trafficking, begar or child labour. (4) Right to Freedom of Religion (Art. 25–28). (5) Cultural and Educational Rights (Art. 29–30): minorities may conserve culture and run institutions. (6) Right to Constitutional Remedies (Art. 32): approach the Supreme Court if rights are violated. They are justiciable but subject to reasonable restrictions.
